messages.content: I want to design an incremental cross-module optimizer that preserves the benefits of cross-module optimization without making cache reuse unsound under symbol interposition. The design needs to match clean-build semantics when dependencies change, when dynamic symbol interposition matters, and when optimized and unoptimized modules are mixed. For a single-module edit, the targets are to halve full-LTO rebuild time while keeping runtime within 5% of full LTO.

That combines a correctness requirement with two performance targets. Incremental reuse should not change the program’s semantics relative to a clean build in any of the stated conditions. At the same time, for single-module edits, the rebuild should take about half the time of a full-LTO rebuild, while the resulting program’s runtime remains within 5% of the full-LTO result. The design challenge is to retain cross-module optimization benefits without reusing an optimization after an assumption it depends on has ceased to be sound.
What does “sound cache reuse” mean here? I do not want incremental compilation to be correct only when the edited module has no outside dependencies.

A cached optimization is sound to reuse only if the assumptions needed for its behavior remain valid for the current build. Those assumptions can concern another module or a symbol whose effective binding may change. So an edit being confined to one module does not, by itself, establish that every cached cross-module result is reusable. Conversely, a dependency change does not necessarily mean that every cached result is unusable; the question is whether the change affects what a particular result relied on.
How should I read the clean-build requirement? Is it asking for identical build artifacts?

The stated requirement is to match clean-build semantics. That is a requirement about the meaning of the resulting program, not an express requirement for byte-for-byte identical artifacts or identical compilation steps. An incremental build must not preserve an assumption merely because it was true in an earlier build if a clean build in the current situation would give the program different semantics.
Why call out dependency changes separately from edits to one module?

Because cross-module optimization can rely on information beyond the module being edited. A dependency change may affect an assumption embodied in cached work even if that work was produced while optimizing another module. The design therefore has to account for relevant changes outside the edited module when deciding whether reuse still matches clean-build semantics. The single-module-edit condition specifies the performance target; it does not narrow the correctness requirement to changes that are purely local.
And what is special about dynamic symbol interposition in that reasoning?

With dynamic symbol interposition, an apparent reference to a symbol is not necessarily a guarantee that one particular definition will be the effective one in every relevant context. If a cached optimization depends on a particular binding, reuse must be justified under the current binding possibilities. Otherwise the incremental result could behave differently from a clean build. This does not make cross-module optimization impossible; it makes the validity of binding-dependent assumptions part of the soundness question.
So is the safe answer simply to avoid any optimization involving an interposable symbol?

That would avoid some risks, but it would not capture the stated goal of preserving optimization benefits. The goal is more precise: retain an optimization when its assumptions are sound, and do not let cached work silently impose an unjustified binding assumption. Nothing in the goal specifies one particular mechanism for making that distinction or says that all uses of an interposable symbol must be treated alike.
I also explicitly included mixed optimized and unoptimized modules. Does that just concern the speed target?

No. Mixed optimized and unoptimized modules are part of the clean-build-semantics requirement. The optimizer cannot rely on every module having been treated the same way to make its cached results correct. Whatever optimization opportunities remain in such a mix, the resulting program must retain the semantics a clean build would have under that mix.
Could you separate the three correctness situations without turning them into three unrelated projects?

They are three ways the same soundness obligation can be tested. A dependency change asks whether reused work still reflects information from other modules. Dynamic symbol interposition asks whether assumptions about effective symbol bindings are warranted. A mix of optimized and unoptimized modules asks whether those assumptions remain correct across differently treated modules. In each case, the central question is whether incremental reuse preserves clean-build semantics.
Suppose an optimization was previously useful, but a relevant assumption is no longer guaranteed. Does the runtime target mean we should keep using it anyway?

No. The runtime target is not permission to weaken semantic correctness. Preserving optimization benefits means pursuing performance within the soundness constraint, not retaining every cached optimization regardless of changed conditions. The design has to meet both aims rather than treating a faster but semantically different result as acceptable.
The phrase “halve full-LTO rebuild time” can be slippery. What comparison is actually stated?

For single-module edits, the stated target is a rebuild time of half the full-LTO rebuild time. That comparison does not, on its own, prescribe a measurement setup or extend the same timing promise to every kind of change. The performance requirement is specific about the edit condition, the full-LTO rebuild baseline, and the factor of two.
And the 5% figure applies to runtime, not build time?

Yes. The two numerical targets measure different things: halve full-LTO rebuild time for a single-module edit, and keep the resulting program’s runtime within 5% of full LTO. Meeting the rebuild-time target alone would not establish the runtime target, and staying close to full-LTO runtime would not establish the rebuild-time target.
Would it be fair to say that a cache decision has to consider what a result depended on, rather than just whether the module containing the result changed?

Yes, as a statement of the soundness problem. A cross-module result can depend on facts beyond the module that contains it, including facts relevant to dependency changes or symbol binding. Merely observing that the containing module is unchanged is therefore not enough to justify reuse in all cases. The goal does not yet choose how the design records or checks those dependencies.
I want to keep that distinction clear: this is a design objective, not a claim that an optimizer has already met the numbers or passed those cases.

Exactly. The requested design should aim for clean-build semantics under dependency changes, dynamic symbol interposition, and mixed optimized/unoptimized modules, while targeting the specified rebuild-time and runtime comparisons for single-module edits. Those are requirements to satisfy, not reported results or a commitment to a particular implementation.

Here is a proposed approach: cache optimized function partitions by dependency and symbol-resolution fingerprints. Inline only definitions that are provably nonpreemptible, and retain calls into unoptimized modules.

That gives cache reuse and cross-module transformation separate safeguards. The fingerprints express which dependency and symbol-resolution conditions a cached optimized function partition relies on. The inlining restriction prevents an optimization from treating a potentially preemptible definition as though it were necessarily the one a call will reach. Retaining calls into unoptimized modules keeps those calls as calls rather than assuming the callee has been incorporated into optimized code.
Can you explain “function partitions” without assuming that each partition is exactly one function?

Yes. The proposal names optimized function partitions as the units being cached; it does not specify that a partition must contain exactly one function. The important point here is the unit of reuse: a cached partition can be considered in light of the dependencies and symbol-resolution assumptions associated with it, rather than declaring all previously optimized work reusable simply because an edited module is elsewhere.
What do the two kinds of fingerprint contribute? I do not want “dependency” to conceal the symbol-interposition issue.

They highlight distinct questions. A dependency fingerprint concerns the information on which an optimized partition depends. A symbol-resolution fingerprint concerns the resolution assumptions relevant to that partition. Calling out symbol resolution explicitly matters because information about a definition is not, by itself, proof that a reference must resolve to that definition when interposition is possible. The proposal does not specify a fingerprint format or claim that any particular fingerprint scheme is sufficient.
If a fingerprint changes, should I describe the old partition as automatically wrong?

Not automatically wrong in its behavior. A changed fingerprint means the proposal cannot justify reusing that cached partition merely on the basis of the earlier fingerprint match. Whether the partition would happen to produce the same behavior is a different question. The conservative distinction is between a result that is established as reusable under the proposal’s conditions and one that is not established as reusable.
And if the fingerprints match, is that already a proof of clean-build semantics?

Not by itself. A match is useful only to the extent that the fingerprints faithfully cover the assumptions that matter to the cached optimization. The proposal is to use dependency and symbol-resolution fingerprints as the basis for reuse, not a claim that matching arbitrary identifiers proves correctness. Sound reuse still depends on capturing the relevant conditions and observing the inlining restriction.
Let us focus on that restriction. What does “provably nonpreemptible” add beyond knowing which definition the optimizer has seen?

It requires a justification that the definition cannot be displaced for the call being optimized. Seeing a definition can make inlining tempting, but it does not alone establish that the definition is the effective target when dynamic symbol interposition matters. Under this proposal, the optimizer inlines only where nonpreemptibility can be proved; otherwise it does not make that inlining assumption.
Is the proposal saying that every reference to a symbol with any possible interposition must prevent all optimization of its surrounding partition?

No. The stated restriction is on inlining definitions without proof of nonpreemptibility. It is not a blanket prohibition on caching or optimizing a partition that contains a call. The broader objective is to preserve optimization benefits while avoiding an unsound binding assumption, and this proposal draws a specific boundary around inlining.
Why explicitly retain calls into unoptimized modules?

Because the proposal has to remain meaningful when optimized and unoptimized modules coexist. Retaining those calls avoids treating an unoptimized callee as though its body had necessarily been incorporated into the optimized partition. It preserves the call boundary in that mixed setting. This is a design rule, not a claim that all behavior of mixed builds has already been verified.
Could a call into an unoptimized module still be part of a cached optimized partition?

The proposal permits an optimized partition to retain such a call. Caching the partition and inlining the callee are different actions: the partition can contain an optimized caller while the call into the unoptimized module remains a call. Any assumptions the cached partition makes about that call still need to be represented appropriately for reuse.
I want to avoid suggesting that “retaining calls” means we somehow get the full benefit of inlining those callees.

That distinction is important. Retaining a call does not supply the benefits of inlining that callee. It is a constraint chosen to avoid making an unsupported transformation at that boundary. The proposal seeks to preserve cross-module optimization benefits where its conditions permit them, without claiming that every possible full-LTO optimization remains available.
How does this approach relate to a single-module edit? Please keep the performance targets framed as targets.

For a single-module edit, caching optimized function partitions offers a way to seek reuse of work whose dependency and symbol-resolution fingerprints remain applicable, instead of necessarily redoing all optimization. That is the proposed route toward halving full-LTO rebuild time. The goal also requires runtime within 5% of full LTO, so restricting inlining and retaining calls have to be considered alongside optimization quality. The proposal alone does not establish either numerical target.
Does “by dependency and symbol-resolution fingerprints” mean one fingerprint per partition, or two separate fingerprints, or something else?

The proposal does not settle their representation or number. It specifies the information that should govern caching: dependencies and symbol-resolution assumptions for optimized function partitions. Those could be represented in different ways, but choosing a representation would be an additional design detail, not something stated here.
Could you describe the clean-build comparison without claiming that a fingerprint match recreates a clean build step for step?

The comparison is semantic. If a cached partition is reused, its use must leave the resulting program with the semantics it would have under a clean build in the current dependency, symbol-resolution, and mixed-module situation. The proposal tries to make that possible by conditioning reuse on the relevant fingerprints and restricting transformations that could presume an unsafe binding. It does not require identical compilation steps or byte-for-byte identical output.
Suppose a dependency changes but does not affect what a partition assumed. Is the proposal intended to leave room for reuse?

Yes, that is the point of associating cached partitions with their dependencies rather than treating every dependency change as necessarily invalidating everything. Reuse would still have to be justified by the relevant dependency and symbol-resolution fingerprints. The proposal does not specify how precisely a dependency’s effect can be isolated in practice.
Conversely, if the edited module is not where a cached partition lives, can the edit still matter to that partition?

Yes. A cached optimized partition can depend on information outside its own location, which is why the dependency and symbol-resolution conditions matter. The proposal bases reuse on those conditions, not solely on whether the partition’s containing module was directly edited.
How narrowly should I state the inlining policy?

State it as: inline only definitions that are provably nonpreemptible. That preserves both parts of the condition: it concerns inlining, and it requires proof of nonpreemptibility rather than an expectation that interposition will not occur. It does not, by itself, prescribe a particular proof method or establish which definitions qualify.
So the proposal is not simply “cache more aggressively,” is it?

No. It pairs conditional reuse of optimized function partitions with limits on the assumptions those partitions may embody. Dependency and symbol-resolution fingerprints address whether cached work remains applicable; inlining only provably nonpreemptible definitions addresses a transformation that can be sensitive to symbol interposition; retaining calls into unoptimized modules addresses the mixed-module boundary. Those pieces are meant to work together, but their adequacy and performance have not been established by stating the proposal.
Which symbol-resolution and visibility facts must enter partition fingerprints to prevent stale inlining after weak-definition or interposition-policy changes?

The fingerprint has to cover the facts on which each inlining decision actually relied. At minimum, that means being able to tell whether the call still resolves to the definition whose body was inlined and whether that definition is still provably nonpreemptible for the call. Relevant facts can include which definition prevails, its weak or strong binding where that affects resolution, the visibility of the reference and definition, and the effective interposition policy and resolution context. The question is about those semantic facts, not a prescribed fingerprint encoding.
Why is recording the identity of the inlined definition insufficient?

Because the same definition can still exist while the justification for calling it changes. A policy change might allow a different definition to interpose, for example, even if the definition originally inlined has not been edited. A fingerprint that records only the body or identity of the inlined definition could miss that change in what the call is permitted to reach.
Does the fingerprint need to distinguish a weak definition from a strong one?

If that distinction matters to the resolution assumption used for inlining, yes. A change involving a weak definition can change which definition prevails without changing the text of the cached partition. But weak binding and dynamic preemptibility are not interchangeable concepts. The fingerprint needs to represent the effective resolution and nonpreemptibility conditions the optimization relied on, rather than treating a single weak-or-strong bit as a complete proof.
What if the previously chosen definition is still present after a weak-definition change?

Its continued presence alone does not establish that the call still reaches it. The relevant question is whether it remains the definition that a clean build would use for that call and whether inlining it remains justified. If a weak-definition change affects either conclusion, reusing the partition with that inlining intact would need fresh justification.
How should visibility enter this? Is it enough to fingerprint the visibility attached to the definition?

Not necessarily. Visibility matters insofar as it affects how a particular reference can bind and whether the selected definition can be preempted. Looking only at the definition may omit a relevant fact about the reference or its resolution context. The fingerprint should cover whichever visibility facts the nonpreemptibility argument for that inlined call depends on; the proposal does not specify a universal field list independent of that argument.
I am concerned about an interposition-policy change that leaves the current selected definition unchanged. Would a fingerprint of the selected definition catch it?

No. The selected definition could look unchanged while the set of definitions that may legally be selected has changed. If the cached partition assumed that another definition could not interpose, the effective interposition policy behind that assumption must be reflected in its reuse conditions. Otherwise an unchanged selected-definition identifier could give false reassurance.
So should the fingerprint contain the policy itself, or just the conclusion that the symbol is nonpreemptible?

Either representation would have to support a sound comparison under the current build conditions. Recording a bare, previously computed conclusion is insufficient if nothing checks whether the facts supporting it still hold. The essential requirement is to re-establish the nonpreemptibility conclusion for the relevant call and inlined definition, whether the fingerprint represents its supporting inputs, a verifiable derived condition, or both. That is a statement of what the fingerprint must establish, not a choice of format.
Is “which definition prevails” a global property of the symbol?

It should not be assumed to be global without regard to resolution context. What matters to an inlining decision is the binding that applies to the particular reference being optimized. If the build’s symbol-resolution rules make context relevant, the fingerprint must not collapse distinct contexts into one apparently matching symbol name.
Would fingerprinting every symbol in every module be the safe interpretation?

That is not required by the question. For a cached partition, the necessary coverage is of the resolution and visibility facts on which its optimizations depend, including facts needed to justify any inlined target. A broader fingerprint could reject reuse unnecessarily; a narrower one is unsound if it omits an assumption that can change the meaning of the cached code. The proposal leaves the desired granularity open.
Can you give me a simple conceptual case, without assuming a particular linker or platform?

Imagine a cached partition in which a call has been replaced with the body of a definition because that definition was established as nonpreemptible for the call. If a change involving a weak definition changes which body that call should reach, a fingerprint that covers only the cached partition’s own code would miss it. Likewise, if an interposition-policy change removes the guarantee that the original body must be called, retaining the inline body without rechecking the guarantee risks differing from a clean build. Those are illustrations of dependencies to track, not claims about any particular platform’s resolution rules.
Should a policy change always discard the partition, even when it cannot affect any inlined call in it?

The soundness requirement is narrower: do not reuse an inlining decision when its justification no longer holds. A coarse fingerprint could conservatively reject the partition on a policy change; a more selective one could permit reuse if it establishes that the partition’s relevant assumptions remain valid. Neither selectivity nor a particular invalidation rule is specified here.
I want to be precise about the word “stale.” Is an old inline body stale merely because a weak definition somewhere changed?

No. It is stale for reuse when the change undermines an assumption needed for that inlining decision—such as the effective target or proof of nonpreemptibility for the relevant call. A weak-definition change elsewhere is not automatically pertinent to every cached partition. The fingerprint’s purpose is to make that distinction without overlooking a relevant change.
How does this interact with the rule to retain calls into unoptimized modules?

Retaining such a call means the partition has not inlined that unoptimized callee, so there is no inlined body for that call to become stale. That does not make symbol resolution irrelevant to every other optimization in the partition. The fingerprint still needs to reflect any resolution or visibility facts the cached partition actually used, while the retained call avoids an unsupported inlining assumption at that boundary.
Can we state the minimum correctness test for reuse without pretending we have enumerated every platform-specific visibility rule?

Yes: for every inlined call in a cached partition, the current build must still justify that the inlined definition is the effective target and is nonpreemptible for that call. The partition fingerprint must be sensitive to changes in the dependency, binding, visibility, resolution-context, and interposition-policy facts that could defeat that justification. The exact facts and their representation depend on the applicable symbol-resolution rules; the correctness test is whether reuse preserves clean-build semantics.
That also means a fingerprint match is meaningful only if those assumptions were included in the first place, correct?

Correct. Matching fingerprints cannot protect against a fact they never represented. In particular, matching the inlined definition’s content is not enough if a weak-definition or interposition-policy change can alter which definition the call may reach. The fingerprint has to cover the assumptions that made the inline substitution sound, not just identify the code that was substituted.

My hypothesis is that recording prevailing-definition identity, linkage strength, visibility, and interposition policy in the partition fingerprint, while forbidding preemptible inlining, prevents stale reuse across weak-definition and DSO changes.

That is a specific proposed answer to the fingerprint question, but it should remain a hypothesis. The recorded facts address both which definition an optimization treated as prevailing and the conditions under which that choice was safe to embed in cached code. The separate prohibition on preemptible inlining limits what the cached partition may assume in the first place. The claim still needs to be assessed against the symbol-resolution rules that apply; naming those facts does not itself prove that every relevant change is detected.
Why include prevailing-definition identity if preemptible inlining is forbidden?

Nonpreemptibility and identity answer different questions. An inlining decision needs both a justified target and a justification that the target cannot be displaced for the relevant call. Recording the prevailing definition’s identity is meant to detect a change in the selected definition; forbidding preemptible inlining is meant to stop the optimizer from embedding a body when its selection is not sufficiently guaranteed. One does not make the other redundant.
What is linkage strength contributing to the hypothesis?

It makes the weak-versus-strong aspect of resolution explicit in the reuse conditions. If a relevant weak-definition change affects which definition prevails, a cached partition should not keep relying on a resolution assumption that no longer holds. The hypothesis is not that linkage strength alone determines the outcome, only that omitting a strength distinction on which the outcome depends could make a fingerprint incomplete.
Could the prevailing-definition identity stay the same while linkage strength changes?

Conceptually, yes: identifying a definition and describing the resolution properties attached to it are distinct. If a change in linkage strength alters a fact the optimization relied on, recording only the identity would not expose that change. The hypothesis includes both so reuse can be conditioned on more than an unchanged identity.
What does visibility add that the first two facts do not?

Visibility can affect whether an apparent target is guaranteed for a particular reference. The identity and linkage strength of a definition do not, on their own, express every condition under which that definition can be treated as nonpreemptible. Recording relevant visibility is intended to prevent reuse from preserving an inlining assumption after the conditions supporting it have changed.
And why record interposition policy separately from visibility?

Because an unchanged visibility description does not necessarily mean the effective interposition rules are unchanged. The hypothesis treats policy as a separate input to whether an inlined definition is safe to assume. Recording it aims to catch a change that alters preemptibility even when the definition’s identity, linkage strength, and visibility appear unchanged.
When I say “forbidding preemptible inlining,” should that be understood as a condition on each call rather than a permanent label on a function?

That is the careful reading. What matters is whether inlining a particular definition at a particular call would rely on a target that can be preempted under the applicable conditions. A definition’s name alone is not a sufficient substitute for that determination. The hypothesis rules out inlining when the required nonpreemptibility is not established.
Does recording these four facts mean the partition can always be reused whenever their recorded values match?

That conclusion would go beyond the hypothesis. A match can support reuse only if those recorded facts capture the relevant assumptions at the necessary scope and are evaluated against the current build conditions. Other dependencies of a cached partition still matter. The hypothesis specifically concerns preventing stale reuse across weak-definition and DSO changes through these symbol-resolution facts and the inlining restriction; it is not a general proof of all partition reuse.
What if a DSO-related change leaves the prevailing-definition identity unchanged?

Then identity alone would not settle the question. Under the hypothesis, the relevant visibility and interposition-policy conditions must also remain suitable for the inlining decision. An unchanged prevailing definition is compatible with a changed justification for assuming that the definition cannot be displaced. Whether a particular DSO change has that effect depends on the applicable resolution rules; the hypothesis aims not to overlook it when it does.
Does the hypothesis claim that every DSO change must invalidate a cached partition?

No. It claims to prevent stale reuse across DSO changes, not to reject reuse after every such change. A change that does not affect the partition’s relevant resolution assumptions need not be treated as though it did. Conversely, a change that alters those assumptions must not be hidden by an overly coarse match. How selectively a fingerprint makes that distinction is not specified in the hypothesis.
Likewise, does every weak-definition change make previously inlined code stale?

Not necessarily. The concern is a weak-definition change that affects the prevailing target or another fact needed to justify the inlining. A weak definition changing somewhere does not, by itself, show that every cached inline substitution has become unsound. The hypothesis is about tracking the pertinent resolution conditions, not treating the word “weak” as a universal invalidation trigger.
Can you state what would count as a failure of the hypothesis without inventing a test result?

A conceptual failure would be a weak-definition or DSO change that allows a cached partition to be reused even though an inlined call no longer has the target or nonpreemptibility required by clean-build semantics. Another would be discovering that one of the supposedly recorded facts was captured at the wrong scope, so a relevant change appeared to match. Those describe ways the hypothesis could fail; they do not assert that either has occurred.
I do not want “recording prevailing-definition identity” to sound like recording only a symbol name.

That distinction matters. A symbol name identifies what is being referenced, but the hypothesis calls for the identity of the prevailing definition—what resolution selected under the relevant conditions. Merely repeating the symbol name could miss a change in which definition prevails. The hypothesis does not prescribe how that identity is encoded.
Could I say that linkage strength and visibility are part of the reason an identity prevails, while interposition policy is part of whether using that identity for inlining is safe?

You can use that as an intuition, provided it is not taken as a complete or universally ordered resolution algorithm. These facts interact under the applicable rules. The hypothesis records all four and separately forbids preemptible inlining precisely because knowing an identity and knowing it is safe to substitute its body are related but distinct requirements.
Is there a risk of overstating this as “a fingerprint solves interposition”?

Yes. A fingerprint is useful only if it represents the facts that justify the cached transformations and is compared under the relevant current conditions. The inlining prohibition is an additional constraint, not something a fingerprint replaces. The narrower hypothesis is that this combination prevents stale reuse across weak-definition and DSO changes; whether it actually does so remains to be established.
How should I describe a policy change that turns a previously safe inline into a preemptible one?

As a case the hypothesis is meant to catch. Even if the inlined body and prevailing-definition identity appear unchanged, a changed interposition policy can remove the justification for treating that definition as fixed at the call. Recording the policy and forbidding preemptible inlining are intended to prevent continued reuse of that inline under the changed conditions. That is the predicted behavior of the hypothesis, not an observed result.
Does “forbidding preemptible inlining” imply that a call with a preemptible target cannot remain in an optimized partition?

No. It restricts substituting a definition’s body for that call. It does not say that an optimized partition cannot contain the call, or that all other optimizations in the partition are disallowed. Keeping the distinction between an optimized partition and a particular inlining decision avoids giving the restriction more scope than the hypothesis states.
I also want to distinguish preventing a stale inline from proving identical generated code to a clean build.

That is appropriate. The hypothesis addresses a semantic hazard: reusing cached code that embeds an inlined target no longer justified under current weak-definition or DSO conditions. Preventing that hazard does not require byte-for-byte identity with a clean build, and the hypothesis does not claim identical generated code. Nor does it, by itself, establish every other condition needed for clean-build semantics.

So the exact proposition is that those four recorded facts, together with the prohibition on preemptible inlining, are sufficient against stale reuse caused by weak-definition or DSO changes—not that sufficiency has been demonstrated?

Yes. Prevailing-definition identity, linkage strength, visibility, and interposition policy are the proposed recorded facts; preemptible inlining is forbidden. The hypothesis is that this combination prevents stale reuse across weak-definition and DSO changes. Its sufficiency is the point to examine, rather than a result already established by stating it.

I want to turn the symbol-resolution question into a concrete plan: enumerate the resolution inputs, key the affected optimized partitions using those inputs, and compare incremental builds with clean builds across weak-definition, DSO, and mixed-mode edits.

That is a plan for examining both cache reuse and its semantic consequences. First identify the resolution and visibility inputs an optimized partition relies on. Then ensure the keys for affected partitions reflect those inputs, so a relevant change cannot look like an unchanged reuse condition. Finally, compare incremental and clean builds under each of the three stated kinds of edits. Those comparisons are planned checks, not results.
What should “enumerate resolution inputs” mean here? I do not want it to mean merely listing symbol names.

It means identifying the facts needed to justify the resolution-dependent optimizations in a partition, not just the names of referenced symbols. For an inlined call, the enumeration would need to address what establishes the effective target and why substituting that definition remains permissible under the applicable visibility and interposition conditions. The plan does not yet claim that a particular list is complete.
Can this enumeration use the prevailing-definition identity, linkage strength, visibility, and interposition policy we have discussed?

Those are the proposed kinds of facts to examine when enumerating the inputs. The plan is to determine which resolution inputs matter to the affected partitions and make them visible to the reuse decision. Including the named categories in that examination does not by itself establish that they capture every relevant distinction or that they are needed in exactly the same form for every partition.
When you say an input matters to a partition, is the idea that an optimization in that partition relied on it?

Yes. The connection should be between an input and an assumption embodied in the cached optimized partition. Otherwise a key might omit a change that matters or include changes unrelated to that partition. The plan calls for keying affected partitions, but it does not specify how fine-grained that association can be made.
Does “key affected partitions” mean assigning a new key only after we discover a mismatch against a clean build?

No. In this plan, keying is part of how reuse is governed in the incremental build. The relevant resolution inputs should be represented in the conditions used to identify reusable optimized partitions. Comparing against clean builds is a separate check on whether that approach preserves the intended semantics; it is not the only way a changed input would become visible.
Should we assume that every edit creates a new key for every optimized partition?

The plan does not require that. It refers to affected partitions: those whose reuse conditions depend on facts changed by the edit. A conservative scheme might treat more partitions as affected, while a more selective one might distinguish unaffected work. Either way, a partition whose relevant resolution assumption changes must not appear reusable on the strength of an unchanged key that omitted that assumption.
I want the order of the plan to be clear. Is enumeration prior to deciding what belongs in a partition key?

Conceptually, yes. Enumerating the inputs establishes what the key needs to represent for the affected partition. Keying without first identifying the assumptions risks a match that says little about sound reuse. The comparison with a clean build then examines whether the incremental result behaves as it should under the current conditions.
How do weak-definition edits fit into that comparison without assuming that every weak change affects every call?

They provide cases where resolution-sensitive assumptions may need to be reconsidered. For each relevant edit, the planned comparison asks whether the incremental build’s reuse decision and resulting semantics agree with a clean build under the changed conditions. The plan does not presuppose that every weak-definition edit changes the effective target, or that every cached partition is affected.
And what do we mean by DSO edits in this plan?

They are the DSO-related edits under which the plan calls for the same incremental-versus-clean comparison. The purpose is to check reuse where symbol resolution or interposition may matter. The node does not prescribe a particular DSO layout, change, or outcome, so the plan should not be read as claiming that any given DSO edit necessarily changes a binding.
Mixed-mode edits seem different from weak and DSO edits. Why include them in the same comparison plan?

The same incremental-versus-clean question applies when optimized and unoptimized modules coexist. The plan includes mixed-mode edits so reuse is examined in that setting too, rather than only where all participating modules are optimized alike. That does not make mixed mode identical to weak-definition or DSO changes; it means all three are within the planned comparisons.
Does “mixed-mode edits” necessarily mean changing a module from optimized to unoptimized or vice versa?

Not necessarily. The phrase establishes that the comparison should cover edits in a mixed optimized/unoptimized setting. It does not specify a particular transition in a module’s optimization mode. Describing such a transition as mandatory would add a condition that is not stated in the plan.
What exactly is compared between an incremental build and a clean build? I do not want to imply byte-for-byte equality.

The essential comparison is whether the incremental result preserves clean-build semantics under the edited conditions. That includes checking the consequences of any cached resolution-dependent optimization rather than assuming that two builds must take identical steps or produce identical bytes. The plan says to compare builds; it does not assert an artifact-identity requirement or report what a comparison has shown.
Could the comparison reveal a problem even if the partition key changes as intended?

Conceptually, yes. Detecting that a reuse condition changed is only one part of obtaining the right resulting program; the incremental build must still have clean-build semantics under the current conditions. The planned comparison examines the result as well as the premise behind reuse. This is a reason to keep keying and clean-build comparison as distinct parts of the plan, not a claim that such a problem has occurred.
Could the opposite happen—a key changes even though the clean-build semantics would be the same?

That is possible in principle with conservative keying. It may decline reuse when a changed recorded input does not ultimately alter the partition’s relevant semantics. The plan is concerned first with preventing unsound reuse; how precisely the keys distinguish affected from unaffected partitions remains open. No selectivity or rebuild-time result follows merely from stating the plan.
I would like to keep the question of preemptible inlining visible without making this plan an implementation specification.

Then frame it as an assumption the enumeration and comparison must account for. I propose extending the resolution-aware partition keys with Merkle-hashed transitive inline-body dependencies. The cache would invalidate affected callers while retaining nonpreemptible-only inlining.

That adds a dependency dimension to the existing resolution-aware reuse condition. The proposal does not prescribe how many levels there are, which functions form a partition, or how the dependency graph is stored. Its concern is that an inline substitution may carry assumptions from farther away than the caller’s direct source.

Merkle hashing expresses the proposal to summarize linked dependencies through hashes: a change in a relevant constituent can change the digest on which a dependent key relies. That can make a transitive dependency relationship available to the reuse decision without describing it as a flat list attached to every caller. The proposal does not specify the shape of the hash structure, the hash function, or a measured benefit over another representation.
Does the Merkle hash replace the symbol-resolution part of a partition key?

No. The proposal explicitly extends resolution-aware partition keys. Resolution conditions still matter to whether an inlined target is valid; the transitive inline-body dependency component addresses whether the body incorporated into cached code remains applicable after changes along its dependency chain. Tracking one does not make the other unnecessary.
Suppose the definition is still nonpreemptible but its relevant inline body has changed transitively. Would the inlining rule alone make the cached caller safe?

No. Nonpreemptibility addresses whether substituting that definition for the call is allowed under the resolution conditions. It does not establish that an already cached copy of its body reflects the current dependencies of that body. The proposed transitive dependency component addresses that separate reuse question.
Conversely, if the inline-body hash is unchanged, can we inline a preemptible definition?

No. A matching body-dependency hash does not establish that the definition is the guaranteed target of the call. The proposal retains nonpreemptible-only inlining, so the resolution condition remains a prerequisite independent of whether the body’s dependency hash matches.
What does “invalidating affected callers” commit us to? I do not want it to imply clearing the entire cache.

It commits the reuse decision to rejecting cached callers whose incorporated inline bodies depend on a changed relevant input. It does not say that every caller, every partition, or the entire cache must be invalidated after any callee edit. The word “affected” is important: the proposed key extension is meant to make the dependency relationship visible where it matters.
Could a caller be affected even if its own source did not change?

Yes. A cached caller may embody an inline body whose relevant dependencies have changed, even when the caller’s own source is untouched. Under the proposal, its key would reflect those transitive inline-body dependencies so that reuse is reconsidered on the basis of what the optimized caller contains, not solely on whether the caller itself was edited.
Does every edit to a callee necessarily change every caller’s key?

Not as stated. The proposal concerns relevant transitive inline-body dependencies of affected callers. A caller that did not incorporate a body depending on the changed information need not be described as affected merely because a callee was edited somewhere. How precisely the hashing distinguishes relevant from unrelated changes is an implementation question the proposal leaves open.
Should “affected caller” mean only a direct caller of the edited callee?

No. That would lose the transitive part of the proposal. A caller can incorporate a body that, in turn, depends on another inline body or other relevant inline-body information. The proposed Merkle-hashed dependency relationship is meant to carry the effect to cached callers that rely on it, even when the edit is not at their immediate call boundary.
I also do not want to imply that merely calling an edited function always creates an inline-body dependency.

That is a useful distinction. The proposal is specifically about dependencies of bodies incorporated through inlining. A call that remains a call is not automatically the same as embedding the callee’s body in the caller. Other conditions may matter to a cached partition’s reuse, but this proposed hash component should not be described as though every call were necessarily an inline-body dependency.
How does the proposal behave conceptually when optimized and unoptimized modules are mixed?

The dependency condition applies to cached callers that actually contain inline bodies, regardless of where a relevant transitive dependency originates. At a boundary where a call remains a call into an unoptimized module, the proposal does not assert that the unoptimized callee was inlined. Clean-build semantics in mixed settings remains the requirement, not an outcome established by this proposal.

No. Merkle hashing can propagate changes through dependencies that are represented in the structure; it cannot reveal an omitted dependency simply by being Merkle-hashed. The proposal specifies the intended approach, not a proof that its dependency coverage is complete.

Invalidating a caller in that situation could be conservative.
