No. EditBench-30 identifies the benchmark; this activity supplies no stratum sizes or count of edits in any group. The number in the name should not be used as a denominator for a hit rate or as a group size.
Why retain “mixed-mode” every time we describe these measurements?

Because the requested measurements are across EditBench-30 edits with optimized and unoptimized modules mixed. A hit rate or rebuild saving measured in that setting should not be described as applying automatically to an optimized-only setting or to every build configuration. The activity does not identify which individual modules have which mode.
Does mixed mode imply every measured edit crosses an optimized-to-unoptimized call boundary?
No. Mixed mode describes the setting, not the location of every edit or call. The activity does not specify which edits touch which modules or whether any particular edit crosses a mode boundary.
If one churn stratum had a different hit rate, would that by itself show why its rebuild time differed?

Not by itself. Hit rates and rebuild savings can be measured side by side, but a difference in one is not automatically the cause of a difference in the other. Rebuild time can include work beyond resolution-summary reuse. The activity requests stratified observations, not a causal attribution or a prediction about their pattern.
Could a high hit rate coexist with modest rebuild savings?

Conceptually, yes: reusing many summaries would not necessarily account for most rebuild time. Conversely, a lower summary hit rate would not by itself determine total rebuild savings. Those are possibilities that explain why both quantities are being measured, not claims about EditBench-30’s results.
Is this activity measuring partition-cache hit rates as well?

Not as stated. It specifically asks for resolution-summary hit rates and rebuild savings. Partition reuse could be relevant to total rebuild time, but the activity does not request a partition-cache hit-rate measurement or provide partition invalidation counts.
Does it include a resulting-program runtime measurement?

No. Its specified measurements are resolution-summary hit rates and rebuild savings, stratified by symbol churn. Neither quantity establishes the resulting program’s runtime relative to full LTO; that would require a separate runtime measurement.
What about clean-build traces—can these measurements establish semantic equivalence?

No. A hit rate says how often summaries are reused, and rebuild savings describe build time. Neither reports whether cached and clean-build traces agree. The activity should not be presented as a semantic-equivalence result.
Could a summary be counted as reusable merely because its fingerprint matches, even if that fingerprint omitted a relevant resolution fact?

A recorded match is only as sound as the facts represented by the fingerprint. The requested hit rate can describe observed reuse under the implemented check, but it does not independently prove that the check captures every relevant symbol-resolution condition. A performance measurement should not be substituted for that correctness argument.
What would this activity let us examine without assuming its outcome?

It would let us examine how resolution-summary reuse and rebuild-time savings vary across the measured symbol-churn strata in mixed-mode EditBench-30 edits. Whether either measure changes with churn, how large any differences are, and what causes them remain open until results are reported and interpreted.
Please state the work precisely in one sentence without supplying measurements or a new experimental design.

Measure resolution-summary hit rates and full-LTO-relative rebuild-time savings for mixed-mode EditBench-30 edits, reporting both by symbol churn; no rates, savings, churn boundaries, or outcomes are specified yet.
The symbol-churn breakdown for mixed-mode EditBench-30 is in: low-churn edits saved 53% in median rebuild time and had 91% resolution-summary hits. High-churn edits had 39% summary hits.

The low-churn group has two reported measurements: 53% median rebuild-time savings and a 91% resolution-summary hit rate. The high-churn group has a reported hit rate of 39%, but no rebuild-savings figure is stated for it. The hit rates differ by 52 percentage points; that difference alone does not tell us the high-churn group’s rebuild time.
What exactly does the 53% measure?

It is the median rebuild-time saving for low-churn edits in the mixed-mode EditBench-30 setting, relative to the rebuild-time comparison baseline. It describes a timing reduction, not the share of summaries reused. It also does not say that every low-churn edit saved exactly 53%.
Can we keep full LTO explicit as that rebuild-time baseline?

Yes. In this EditBench-30 comparison, the low-churn group’s reported median rebuild-time saving is 53% versus full LTO. The 91% and 39% figures have a different basis: they are resolution-summary hit rates within their respective symbol-churn groups.
Would it be accurate to say the low-churn median rebuild took 47% of the full-LTO time?

That is an equivalent way to express a 53% median saving relative to full LTO. Keep the median qualification: it does not imply that every low-churn rebuild took 47% as long as its full-LTO counterpart.
What does the 91% count? I do not want to call it a percentage of edit cases without support.

It is a resolution-summary hit rate for the low-churn mixed-mode edits. The result does not specify its counting denominator, such as a number of individual edits or summary lookups. It should not be recast as saying that 91% of edits met a timing target.
And the 39% belongs only to high-churn edits?

Yes. The reported 39% resolution-summary hit rate is for high-churn edits. It is not an overall hit rate for all mixed-mode EditBench-30 edits, and it does not supply a high-churn rebuild-savings percentage.
Can I say high-churn rebuilds saved 39%?
No. That would confuse a summary hit rate with a rebuild-time saving. The high-churn finding reports 39% hits; it gives no high-churn median rebuild-time saving.
Could I describe the 91% and 39% figures as a 52% reduction in hit rate?

The unambiguous comparison is a difference of 52 percentage points between the reported hit rates: 91% minus 39%. Calling it a 52% reduction would suggest a relative percentage change, which is a different calculation.
Does the gap prove that symbol churn caused fewer summary hits?

The stratified results show different hit rates in the low-churn and high-churn groups. They do not, on their own, establish a causal explanation for the difference or identify which resolution facts prevented reuse. The observation should remain a comparison between the reported groups.
Do the two low-churn figures establish that the summary hits caused the 53% saving?

No. The 91% hit rate and the 53% median rebuild-time saving were both observed for low-churn mixed-mode edits, but the finding does not isolate the contribution of summary reuse to rebuild time. Other rebuild work is not quantified here.
Can we infer the median rebuild saving for all mixed-mode edits from the low-churn figure?

Not from this breakdown. The 53% median applies to low-churn edits, and there is no reported rebuild-saving value for high-churn edits or a combined value in this finding. Combining strata would require information not supplied here.
Does the result give the number of edits in either churn group?

No. It names low-churn and high-churn groups but does not give their sizes, the thresholds defining them, or the number of observations behind either hit rate. The benchmark name does not fill in those missing counts.
What if someone says 91% hits means clean-build semantics were verified in 91% of cases?

That would conflate cache reuse with semantic comparison. A summary hit rate describes how often a cached resolution summary was treated as reusable under the measurement’s counting rule. This finding reports no clean-build trace comparisons or semantic-equivalence percentage for either churn group.
Does the 53% figure say anything about resulting-program runtime?
No. It is a median rebuild-time saving. Neither that figure nor either summary hit rate measures execution time of the resulting program relative to full LTO.
Should we assume that low churn means no symbol-resolution facts changed?
No. “Low-churn” identifies a stratum, not an assertion of zero symbol changes. The finding does not define the churn boundaries or specify the changes within either group.
Is it possible to state what the evidence supports without making a claim about a remedy or its universal performance?

Yes. In mixed-mode EditBench-30, the low-churn edits showed 53% median rebuild-time savings versus full LTO and a 91% resolution-summary hit rate; the high-churn edits showed a 39% resolution-summary hit rate. That supports a comparison of the observed hit rates, while leaving high-churn rebuild savings, runtime, causation, and behavior outside these observations unstated.
Let’s retain resolution-summary caching for low-churn edits, but optimize high-churn resolution, because mixed-mode rebuild savings remain 47% overall.

That makes the decision two-part: keep summary caching for low-churn edits, and direct optimization work toward resolution in high-churn edits. The stated reason is that overall mixed-mode rebuild savings remain 47%. It does not specify how high-churn resolution will be optimized or predict a new savings figure.
Does “retain” mean we are committing to summary caching for every kind of edit?
No. The decision specifically says to retain it for low-churn edits. It does not decide whether summaries should be cached, recomputed, or handled another way for every high-churn edit.
I also do not want “optimize high-churn resolution” to be mistaken for a decision to loosen the cache-validity checks.

It need not be read that way. The decision identifies resolution work under high symbol churn as the optimization focus, without specifying a method. It does not authorize reuse of a resolution summary when its fingerprint no longer supports reuse, or otherwise relax soundness under symbol interposition.
What is the distinction between retaining the cache and optimizing resolution?

Retaining summary caching preserves that existing way of reusing applicable resolution information for low-churn edits. Optimizing high-churn resolution is a direction for further work where resolution conditions change more. The decision does not say that the second action must use the same caching approach as the first.
Is the 47% a resolution-summary hit rate?

No. It is the overall mixed-mode rebuild-time saving, relative to full LTO. A summary hit rate measures reuse opportunities; rebuild savings measure time. The reason for the decision uses the overall timing figure, not a 47% hit rate.
Should we call that 47% the saving for each high-churn edit?

No. “Overall” matters: the 47% applies to mixed-mode rebuild savings as a whole in the stated result. The decision does not give a separate rebuild-saving figure for high-churn edits or claim that each edit saved the same amount.
Does the decision say high-churn resolution caused the overall saving to be 47%?

It selects high-churn resolution as the area to optimize because overall mixed-mode savings remain 47%. It does not establish a causal breakdown of that overall figure or quantify how much time high-churn resolution accounts for. The focus of the decision should not be turned into an attribution the decision does not make.
Could “optimize high-churn resolution” be described as a completed performance improvement?

No. It is a decision about where to direct optimization, not a report that the optimization has been implemented or measured. The only performance figure stated in the decision is the existing 47% overall mixed-mode rebuild saving.
Are we abandoning resolution-summary caching altogether because overall savings are 47%?
No. The decision expressly retains summary caching for low-churn edits. Its response to the overall 47% figure is not to discard that caching, but to focus optimization on high-churn resolution.
Can we state what “low-churn” and “high-churn” mean numerically here?

Not from this decision. They identify the two symbol-churn conditions to treat differently, but no churn thresholds or classification rule are specified. Assigning a numerical cutoff would add an implementation detail.
What if a mixed-mode rebuild contains both low-churn and high-churn work?

The decision distinguishes the treatment of low-churn edits from the optimization focus for high-churn resolution. It does not specify how to classify a rebuild with different kinds of changes within it, or how to divide work inside such a rebuild. Those details remain unspecified.
Why keep the word “mixed-mode” attached to the 47%?

Because the stated overall saving is for the mixed optimized/unoptimized setting. Omitting that condition could make the 47% sound like a result for every EditBench-30 configuration. The decision gives no universal rebuild-saving figure.
Does this choose a particular way to make high-churn resolution faster, such as a new summary format?

No. It chooses the area of work, not a technique. A new format, a different cache policy, or any other particular mechanism would be an additional proposal. This decision alone supplies no design or measured effect for high-churn resolution optimization.
And should the transitive inline-body dependency checks still matter when resolution work is optimized?

Yes, conceptually those are separate soundness concerns. Optimizing the work of resolving symbols does not, by itself, make dependencies of cached inline bodies current. The decision does not say to remove dependency-aware reuse conditions or to permit preemptible inlining.
Does the decision settle the resulting program’s runtime relative to full LTO?

No new runtime result or runtime decision is stated here. The 47% concerns overall mixed-mode rebuild savings, not execution speed. Nothing in the decision predicts what runtime would be after optimizing high-churn resolution.
Could I phrase this as ‘summary caching works for low churn, but fails for high churn’?

That would assert more than the decision does. It says to retain summary caching for low-churn edits and optimize high-churn resolution; it does not declare caching a categorical success or failure in either condition. Keeping the phrasing as a choice of treatment and focus avoids inventing a broader evaluation.
What, then, is the precise reason attached to this choice?

The explicit reason is that overall mixed-mode rebuild savings remain 47%. That motivates retaining the low-churn summary cache while focusing further optimization on high-churn resolution. It does not specify why the overall result has that value or how much the proposed focus will change it.
I want a concise decision statement with the number and its scope intact.

Retain resolution-summary caching for low-churn edits and focus optimization on high-churn resolution, because overall mixed-mode rebuild-time savings remain 47% versus full LTO. The high-churn optimization method and its outcome are not specified.
I propose maintaining a per-symbol resolution dependency graph. Recompute resolution summaries only for changed bindings and their dependents, while preserving interposition-aware invalidation.

That is a selective-recomputation proposal. The graph would express which resolution summaries depend on which symbol bindings, so a changed binding prompts recomputation of its summary and dependent summaries rather than an indiscriminate recomputation. The constraint is that this selectivity must not let a change relevant to symbol interposition escape invalidation. The proposal does not yet establish a performance or correctness result.
Why make the graph per-symbol rather than simply tracking whether a module changed?

A module edit and a change relevant to a particular symbol’s resolution are not the same condition. Per-symbol tracking aims to identify the resolution information that depends on a changed binding without treating every summary associated with a module as necessarily affected. That is the intended granularity of the proposal, not a claim that a particular graph has already achieved it.
What should an edge in the dependency graph mean? I do not want to commit to a particular graph representation.

Conceptually, it should mean that the applicability of one piece of resolution information depends on another binding or resolution condition. Following the dependency relationship would identify summaries that must be reconsidered when that condition changes. The proposal does not specify how edges are stored, how dependencies are discovered, or an exact direction in an implementation’s data structure.
Does “dependents” include indirect dependents?

It should include dependents reached through the relevant dependency relationships, not just immediately associated summaries, if an indirect dependency can affect resolution information being reused. Otherwise the graph could stop propagation before reaching a summary that relies on the changed binding. The proposal does not specify a traversal algorithm or the depth of any particular dependency chain.
When I say “recompute only for changed bindings and dependents,” am I saying that every other summary is definitely safe?

Only if the graph and its invalidation conditions faithfully represent all resolution dependencies relevant to those summaries. The proposal is to avoid recomputing summaries that are genuinely unaffected. It would not be sound to call a summary unaffected merely because a relevant dependency was omitted from the graph.
How do cached summaries fit into this without making the graph a replacement for their fingerprints?

The graph can identify which resolution summaries need reconsideration after a binding change, while a fingerprint can express conditions for reusing a particular cached summary. Those are complementary roles. The proposal does not say to remove fingerprints or to reuse a saved summary simply because the graph did not flag it; the dependency tracking has to support the same sound reuse conditions.
Could the graph also replace the transitive inline-body Merkle keys?

That is not part of the proposal. A per-symbol resolution dependency graph concerns resolution summaries and changed bindings. Transitive inline-body dependencies concern whether bodies incorporated into cached optimized code remain current. Selectively recomputing resolution information does not, by itself, address every dependency of an inlined body.
What does “changed binding” mean if a definition’s code changes but symbol resolution does not?

The proposal specifically targets recomputation of resolution summaries for changed bindings and their dependents. A code-body change without a resolution change may still matter to cached optimized code, but it should not be silently redescribed as a binding change merely to make this graph cover it. The per-symbol resolution graph does not replace checks for inline-body dependencies.
And what if an interposition-policy change leaves the currently selected definition looking the same?

That is why the interposition-aware qualification matters. An unchanged apparent selection is not always sufficient to preserve an assumption that the definition cannot be displaced. If a policy change affects the resolution conditions on which a cached summary or optimization relies, the invalidation scheme must recognize that relevance. A graph keyed only to changes in the current definition’s identity would not necessarily do so.
Is that inconsistent with saying to recompute only for changed bindings and dependents?

It calls for a careful reading of what counts as a relevant binding change. The condition cannot be reduced to a different symbol name or a different currently selected definition if an interposition change alters the binding guarantees that a summary represents. Selective recomputation remains the aim, but the changes propagated through the graph must include resolution conditions relevant to sound interposition-aware reuse.
Does the proposal require recomputing every summary whenever DSO-related conditions change?

No. It aims to identify the summaries affected by changed bindings or their dependents while preserving interposition-aware invalidation. A change should not be ignored when it affects a summary’s assumptions, but neither does the proposal call for automatically recomputing every summary for every DSO-related change. How precisely affected summaries can be identified remains an open design matter.
Could you distinguish recomputing a resolution summary from invalidating an optimized partition?

Recomputing a summary updates resolution information after a relevant change. Invalidating an optimized partition rejects reuse of cached code when an assumption embodied in that code no longer holds. A changed resolution summary may inform whether a partition remains reusable, but the two actions are not identical. The proposal focuses on selective summary recomputation while requiring interposition-aware invalidation to remain sound.
If a dependent summary is recomputed, does that automatically mean every partition using it must be discarded?

Not automatically. Recomputing the summary establishes current resolution information; a partition’s reuse depends on whether the assumptions it actually used still hold. The proposal does not specify a rule that every recomputation forces every associated partition to be invalidated. It does require that a relevant changed interposition assumption not be concealed by the selective-recomputation scheme.
Likewise, if a summary did not need recomputation, is a cached partition necessarily reusable?

No. The partition may have other dependencies, including inline-body dependencies, that affect reuse independently of symbol resolution. A current resolution summary addresses one class of assumptions. It is not a general certificate that every cached optimization in a partition remains applicable.
What happens at a call that remains a call into an unoptimized module?

The per-symbol graph can still matter if a cached resolution summary depends on the binding conditions for that call. But a retained call should not be treated as though the unoptimized callee’s body had been inlined. The proposal does not change the distinction between resolution dependencies and inline-body dependencies in a mixed optimized/unoptimized build.
Does this proposal change the rule against preemptible inlining?

No. Selective recomputation of resolution summaries does not turn a preemptible definition into a safe inline target. Interposition-aware invalidation and the restriction to nonpreemptible-only inlining continue to address whether cached code may embody a particular binding assumption.
Why might this approach matter for rebuild time, without predicting a percentage?

If resolution summaries can be recomputed only where changed bindings or their dependents require it, unaffected summaries could remain available instead of being recomputed. That is the proposed way to reduce resolution work during incremental rebuilds. The proposal contains no measurement of how much time this would save.
Can we say it achieves at least 50% median mixed-mode rebuild savings on EditBench-30?

No. That would require benchmark results for an implementation of this approach. Maintaining a per-symbol graph and limiting recomputation is a proposed mechanism; it does not supply an EditBench-30 median rebuild-time saving or establish the broader target of halving full-LTO rebuild time for single-module edits.
Does it tell us anything about the resulting program’s runtime versus full LTO?

Not quantitatively. The proposal changes how resolution information is maintained during incremental rebuilding while preserving sound invalidation. It does not report execution-time measurements or establish that resulting-program runtime stays within 5% of full LTO.
What would be an unsound interpretation of “only” in the recomputation rule?

It would be unsound to interpret “only” as permission to skip a summary when a relevant interposition condition changes but the graph fails to represent that condition. “Only” expresses the desired selectivity among genuinely unaffected and affected summaries. It does not override the requirement to invalidate cached assumptions when symbol resolution may have changed in a way that matters.
Should we state that the graph has already identified all relevant dependents?

No. This is a proposal to maintain such a graph. It does not report that the dependency relationships have been fully enumerated, that an implementation exists, or that interposition-aware invalidation has been demonstrated under it.
Put the proposal in one sentence without making it sound like an implemented or measured fix.

Maintain a per-symbol resolution dependency graph so resolution summaries are recomputed only for changed bindings and their dependents, while ensuring that relevant interposition changes still invalidate cached assumptions; this remains a proposal, not a measured result.
How can the resolution graph detect weak-winner and DSO preload changes without invalidating partitions that depend on unrelated symbols?

The key distinction is between detecting a changed resolution condition and propagating its effect only to work that depends on it. The graph would need to notice when a weak-winner change or a DSO preload change alters a binding or an interposition assumption. It would then identify resolution summaries and cached partitions that rely on that condition. A partition whose assumptions concern unrelated symbols should not be invalidated solely because some other symbol changed. This describes what a sound, selective graph needs to accomplish, not a completed design.
What exactly would count as a weak-winner change for this purpose?

The relevant event is a change in which definition prevails for a symbol under the applicable resolution conditions. If a cached summary or partition assumed the previous prevailing definition, that assumption needs to be reconsidered. The graph must associate the changed resolution fact with its dependents rather than treating every cached partition as dependent on every weak definition.
Could we detect it just by checking whether the source of a partition changed?

No. A partition can rely on the prevailing definition of a symbol whose source is elsewhere. Its own source may be unchanged while its resolution assumption changes. The graph is intended to represent that dependency so the reuse decision is not based only on where an edit occurred.
Would recording the identity of the current winner be enough to detect a DSO preload change?

Not necessarily. A preload change may alter which definition a reference reaches, but it may also alter an interposition condition relevant to whether a particular target can be assumed fixed, even if an apparent winner remains the same. Detection therefore has to cover the resolution or preemptibility facts a cached optimization actually relied on, not only a saved winner identity.
Does that mean every change in DSO preload has to invalidate every partition?

No. The question specifically asks for selectivity. A preload change must be reflected where it affects a symbol-resolution assumption used by a summary or partition. It does not follow that a partition depending only on unrelated symbols must be discarded. The difficult part is representing the relevant dependence accurately enough to make that distinction soundly.
What does it mean for a partition to depend on a symbol in this question?

It means the cached optimized code relies on a fact about that symbol’s resolution—for example, which definition is used or whether an inlined definition is nonpreemptible for a particular call. Merely containing a symbol name does not establish which resolution facts the optimization used. The graph needs to track pertinent assumptions, including dependencies reached indirectly where they matter.
Why mention indirect dependencies? Wouldn’t a per-symbol graph link each partition straight to every symbol it cares about?

That is one conceivable representation, but the question does not prescribe it. A partition might rely on a resolution summary that itself depends on another binding. Whether the implementation links a partition directly to each relevant condition or follows dependencies through summaries, it must not stop propagation before reaching an affected partition. Equally, it should not label an unrelated partition affected merely because it shares some broader module or build context.
Can a graph keyed only by symbol names give us the distinction we need?

Names can identify the symbols under discussion, but they are not always the entire resolution condition. The effective binding and the justification for inlining may depend on the applicable visibility, strength, interposition policy, or reference context. If two materially different conditions collapse into the same name, an unchanged-looking graph entry could miss a relevant weak-winner or preload change. The required precision depends on the assumptions actually made.
What if a weak-winner change concerns a symbol that a partition merely calls but has not inlined?

It should not automatically be treated as a stale-inline dependency for that partition. A retained call and an embedded inline body are different. But if some other optimization or cached resolution information in that partition relied on a fact about the call’s target, that reliance still matters. The graph should track the relevant assumption, rather than declaring every call either affected or unaffected by definition.
How do we avoid invalidating an unrelated partition when a broad interposition policy changes?

The graph would need a way to distinguish which cached assumptions are subject to the changed policy. If a partition’s justification depends on that policy, it must be reconsidered even if its selected definition looks unchanged. If the policy change cannot affect any resolution assumption the partition used, treating it as unrelated would preserve reuse. The question does not establish how finely a particular implementation can make that distinction.
So could there be a policy change without a winner change that still matters to an inline?

Yes, conceptually. The body currently selected could be the same, while the guarantee that it cannot be preempted changes. For an inline substitution, the guarantee matters as well as the current definition’s identity. A graph that observes only winner changes could miss that kind of dependency.
What should happen when the graph detects a changed binding?

It should make summaries dependent on the changed binding subject to recomputation, including relevant indirect dependents. A cached partition relying on a changed resolution assumption must then be reconsidered for reuse. Detecting that a summary needs recomputation and deciding that a partition must be invalidated are related but distinct decisions: updated information might leave a partition’s assumptions applicable, or it might not.
Does recomputing a summary necessarily invalidate all partitions that consulted it?

Not necessarily. Recomputing establishes current resolution information; invalidating a cached partition depends on whether that partition’s recorded assumptions still hold. An implementation could be conservative, but a summary-recomputation event alone is not proof that every dependent optimized partition has stale code. Nor is the absence of a recorded dependency proof that a partition is safe if the graph omitted an assumption.
What does an unrelated symbol mean when there is a dependency chain through summaries?

It means the changed symbol’s binding or interposition conditions cannot affect the resolution assumptions used by that partition, whether directly or through a relevant chain of summaries. The label should be based on the dependency relationship, not simply on different symbol names or different source modules. Otherwise an indirect dependence could be mistaken for no dependence.
Could a preload affect several symbols at once without forcing global invalidation?

In principle, yes. The graph could treat each relevant changed resolution condition as a starting point and consider the union of its dependents. That would allow several symbols’ affected partitions to be reconsidered without automatically including partitions dependent only on unrelated symbols. This is a conceptual selectivity rule, not a claim about how many symbols any particular preload changes.
Would it be sound to decide which symbols changed by comparing only the currently prevailing definitions before and after preload?

That may miss a change to preemptibility or another binding guarantee on which cached code relies. The comparison needs to be sensitive to the resolution conditions represented by the summaries and partitions. A changed prevailing definition is clearly relevant when that definition was assumed, but an unchanged prevailing identity is not a universal certificate that all relevant assumptions remain valid.
Where does nonpreemptible-only inlining enter the answer?

It narrows which binding assumptions can be embedded as inline bodies. A partition should not contain an inline based on a preemptible target. For a permitted inline, however, the graph still needs to detect a weak-winner or DSO preload change that undermines the target or its nonpreemptibility justification. The inlining restriction and selective dependency propagation serve different purposes.
Does this graph make the transitive inline-body Merkle keys unnecessary?

No. The resolution graph concerns changes in symbol binding and dependents of resolution summaries. Merkle keys for transitive inline-body dependencies address whether cached bodies reflect their relevant callee dependencies. A partition may need both sorts of reuse condition. Calling a symbol unrelated for resolution purposes does not automatically settle every other dependency of its cached code.
What would an overly broad graph do, and what would an overly narrow one do?

An overly broad graph could cause unnecessary summary recomputation and partition invalidation when weak-winner or preload changes affect unrelated symbols. An overly narrow graph could fail to propagate a changed binding or interposition condition to a partition that relied on it, making stale reuse possible. The question asks how to find a sound boundary between those two outcomes; it does not state that a particular boundary has been implemented.
If we cannot confidently establish whether a partition depends on a changed resolution condition, can we assume it is unrelated to save rebuild time?

No. The benefit of retaining it does not justify an unsupported reuse assumption. Selectivity requires evidence that the partition’s relevant resolution conditions remain applicable. When that cannot be established, a conservative decision may reject reuse; the question remains how to represent dependencies precisely enough to avoid unnecessary rejection without missing an affected partition.
Would clean-build trace comparisons answer whether the graph strikes that balance?

They can test whether cached results agree with clean builds in the conditions exercised, but trace agreement alone does not show that unrelated partitions stayed cached. To assess both sides of the question, one would examine semantic agreement and which summaries or partitions were reconsidered after weak-winner and DSO preload changes. No new comparisons or outcomes are stated in this question.
Can we give a small conceptual illustration without inventing a platform-specific resolution rule?

Suppose one cached partition inlines a definition of symbol A under a nonpreemptibility assumption, while another partition’s recorded resolution assumptions concern only symbol B. If a weak-winner or preload change affects the assumption about A but cannot affect those about B, propagation should reach the A-dependent partition and leave the B-only partition eligible for reuse on that basis. The illustration assumes the graph has correctly captured all relevant relationships; it does not claim that any particular preload or weak change necessarily behaves this way.
What is the most concise answer to the question, while keeping it open rather than pretending the graph has already solved it?

Track the binding and interposition conditions on which each resolution summary and cached partition depends; detect weak-winner and DSO preload changes to those conditions; and propagate reconsideration through their relevant dependents, not to partitions whose assumptions concern unrelated symbols. The open design question is how completely and precisely the per-symbol graph can represent those dependencies while preserving clean-build semantics.

My hypothesis is to fingerprint link-time candidate sets and preemptibility policy per symbol, retain dynamic calls, and invalidate only dependents of changed bindings. Could that let the resolution graph detect weak-winner and DSO preload changes without invalidating partitions that depend on unrelated symbols?

That is a proposed way to combine sensitivity with selectivity, not an established result. The per-symbol fingerprints would represent the link-time candidates and the preemptibility policy relevant to resolution; retaining dynamic calls would avoid substituting an assumed body at those call sites. When a binding changes, the graph would direct invalidation to its dependents rather than every partition. Whether those recorded facts fully capture relevant weak-winner and DSO preload changes remains to be established.
Why fingerprint a link-time candidate set rather than just the prevailing definition?

A prevailing-definition identity describes a selection, whereas the candidate set describes the link-time definitions among which resolution is considered. A change to the candidates may be relevant to a binding even if looking only at a previously recorded identity would not expose the underlying change. The hypothesis is to make that candidate-set information visible to the reuse check; it does not claim that every candidate-set change necessarily changes an effective binding.
Does a fingerprint of the candidate set tell us which candidate wins?

Not by itself. A fingerprint can represent whether the recorded candidate set is the same under the chosen comparison, but it is not a replacement for applying the relevant resolution conditions. The proposed invalidation rule still hinges on changed bindings and their dependents. Treating every changed candidate set as proof of a changed winner, or every matching candidate set as a complete resolution proof, would overstate the hypothesis.
What does the ‘per symbol’ qualifier apply to?

It applies to the proposed candidate-set and preemptibility-policy fingerprints. Instead of making one undifferentiated fingerprint for all symbols, the hypothesis associates those resolution inputs with the symbols to which they pertain. Does it make a preemptible call safe to inline?

Why rerun fresh-seed EditBench-30 instead of estimating the savings from the number of commits?

I propose reusing unchanged partitions across epoch-retried links, but validating their dependency fingerprints against the committed snapshot before final linking.

That separates an epoch-triggered link retry from an automatic decision to rebuild every partition. An unchanged partition remains a candidate for reuse across the retry, but its dependency fingerprint must be valid against the committed snapshot before it is included in the final link. This is a proposal for conditional reuse, not a claim that the checks have been implemented or measured.
Does “unchanged partition” mean a partition whose source text is unchanged?

Source text alone is not sufficient. A partition can be unchanged as a cached object while assumptions it relied on have changed elsewhere. Under this proposal, retaining it across a retry is permitted only if its relevant dependency fingerprint validates against the committed snapshot.
So should we describe unchanged partitions as automatically safe to reuse?

No. “Unchanged” identifies candidates whose cached work might be retained. The validation condition determines whether that work can actually be used in the final linked result. Calling all unchanged partitions safe would remove the qualification that makes the proposal soundness-conscious.
Why reuse across epoch-retried links rather than throw away everything when the epoch changes?

An epoch change can require a link attempt to reconsider its resolution view without necessarily changing every dependency of every cached partition. The proposal preserves a chance to reuse partitions whose assumptions still validate against the committed snapshot. It does not promise that any particular retry will retain a specified number of partitions or save a specified amount of time.
Does this proposal say we always reuse at least one partition on a retry?
No. Reuse depends on the validation results. If no partition’s relevant dependencies remain valid, the proposal does not require retaining one merely to show that reuse occurred.
What does “committed snapshot” contribute to the comparison?

It supplies the resolution view against which the dependency conditions are checked for the final link. A partition should not be accepted solely because its fingerprint matched an earlier view used by a link attempt that was retried. The proposal does not specify the snapshot’s representation or the process by which it is committed.
Could the snapshot change while a partition is being checked?

The proposed check is against a committed snapshot, so the comparison should have a consistent reference rather than silently shifting between resolution views. That describes the necessary meaning of validation here; it does not prescribe a synchronization technique or a particular lifetime for the snapshot.
Are we validating the partition fingerprint against the epoch number alone?

That is not what the proposal states. It calls for validating dependency fingerprints against the committed snapshot. An epoch can signal that a link needs to reconsider its view, but an epoch number alone would not necessarily establish that a particular partition’s recorded dependencies still hold. The proposal leaves the exact fingerprint comparison unspecified.
Does a newer epoch necessarily invalidate every dependency fingerprint?

No. The retry makes the final link reconsider its applicable snapshot; it does not prove every cached partition depends on what changed. The proposed validation is meant to distinguish unchanged partitions whose dependencies remain valid from those whose assumptions no longer apply.
What if a partition’s fingerprint does not validate against the committed snapshot?

Then that partition cannot be reused for the final link on the strength of its cached version. The proposal does not prescribe what precise rebuilding or retry work follows a failed validation. Its explicit boundary is that final linking must not use the partition with an unsupported dependency assumption.
And if the fingerprint validates, does that guarantee the whole program matches a clean build?

Not by itself. The check can support reuse only if the fingerprint represents the dependencies the partition actually relies on and the snapshot supplies the relevant current facts. Every other partition and applicable condition still matters. The proposal does not report clean-build comparisons or claim a universal semantic guarantee from one matching fingerprint.
What kinds of dependencies are meant here? Should I enumerate specific fields in the proposal?

The proposal says “dependency fingerprints” without defining a field list. Their essential role is to cover the assumptions necessary to reuse the cached partition under the committed resolution view. Stating a particular encoding or a complete set of fields would add an implementation choice that is not specified.
Is symbol interposition relevant even when the partition’s own code has not changed?

Yes. A partition may embody an assumption about which definition a call can reach or whether an inlined definition is nonpreemptible. Those assumptions can be affected by resolution conditions outside the partition. Rechecking dependencies against the committed snapshot is meant to prevent unchanged cached code from carrying an invalid binding assumption into the final link.
Does validation make it permissible to inline a preemptible definition?

No. Validating that a cached partition’s dependencies still apply does not make an intrinsically unjustified fixed-target substitution sound. The proposal concerns reuse of partitions across link retries; it does not propose relaxing the restriction on preemptible inlining.
Does it require inlining calls into unoptimized modules to preserve performance?

No. Retaining or reusing a partition is different from inlining every call it contains. The proposal does not change the treatment of calls into unoptimized modules, and no particular inlining choice follows from a fingerprint match.
How does this apply if a dependency changes while the link is being retried?

The reuse decision for the final link has to be made relative to the committed snapshot used for that link, not solely relative to a view from before the retry. If a change defeats a partition’s recorded dependencies, validation should prevent its cached version from being used. The proposal does not specify the timing of further changes or a detailed procedure for multiple retries.
Could a partition remain in the cache even if it cannot be used in the current final link?

The proposal distinguishes keeping cached work available from accepting it for final linking. It says to reuse unchanged partitions across epoch-retried links subject to validation; it does not prescribe a cache-eviction policy. Failure to validate means the cached partition is not justified for this final link, regardless of whether a stored entry remains.
Does this involve validating fingerprints before or after final linking?

Before final linking. That ordering is explicit: the dependency fingerprints are validated against the committed snapshot before the partitions are accepted into the final linked result. Checking afterward would not provide the stated pre-link reuse condition.
Is this just the same as checking symbol-resolution fingerprints before final link?

The proposal is specifically about validating the dependency fingerprints of unchanged partitions against the committed snapshot when a link has been retried on an epoch change. Symbol-resolution conditions may be among the facts relevant to reuse, but the central distinction is that each candidate partition’s dependencies must be checked for the final attempt, not presumed applicable because it was available during an earlier attempt.
What happens to partitions that actually changed?

The reuse rule here is limited to unchanged partitions across epoch-retried links. It does not prescribe a processing rule for changed partitions or say that they become reusable through this particular validation. Extending the claim to all partitions would exceed the proposal.
Does the proposal assume that a retry always entails recompiling changed partitions in parallel?

No such scheduling condition is included. It identifies which cached partitions may be reused across epoch-retried links and when their fingerprints are validated. It does not specify worker counts, partition assignments, or how work excluded from reuse is scheduled.
Could we say that the committed snapshot proves the absence of all dependency changes?

No. A committed snapshot provides a consistent reference for validation; it is not an assertion that nothing has changed. Indeed, a retry may occur precisely because the earlier resolution view cannot simply be carried forward. The fingerprint check asks whether each candidate partition’s own dependencies remain applicable under the committed view.
What is the soundness failure we are trying not to introduce by keeping work across a retry?

The risk is carrying a cached partition into the final link after an epoch-related change has invalidated an assumption it embodies. Merely keeping the partition unchanged in the cache cannot justify that. Validation against the committed snapshot is the proposed gate between retaining a candidate and actually reusing it.
Would refusing to reuse any partition across a retry satisfy this proposal?

That would avoid some reuse risks, but it would not express the proposal’s optimization aim: reuse unchanged partitions when their dependency fingerprints validate. The proposal is neither unconditional retention nor unconditional rejection after an epoch change. It seeks sound, selective reuse.
Does this tell us whether the rebuild-time target is achieved?

No. Preserving validated work across retries is a proposed way to avoid unnecessary rebuilding, but the statement provides no elapsed times. It does not establish that single-module edits halve full-LTO rebuild time.
And can we infer the resulting program will stay within 5% of full-LTO runtime?
No. Conditional reuse and pre-link validation do not provide a program-runtime measurement. The within-5% runtime goal remains separate from the mechanism described here.
Could correct validation be inferred from matching traces in a named benchmark?

A trace comparison would provide behavioral evidence for the cases compared, but this proposal states no new experiment, trace count, or result. Nor would a trace match alone enumerate the partition fingerprints checked or establish completeness for every possible dependency.
Can you state the whole proposal in one sentence, keeping the epoch retry and final-link order explicit?

Across epoch-retried links, reuse unchanged partitions only when their dependency fingerprints validate against the committed snapshot before final linking; the proposal does not yet establish semantic or performance outcomes.
Can snapshot-validated retry reuse recover fresh-seed rebuild savings above 50% without admitting stale partitions after concurrent weak-winner changes?

That is an open question with two conditions. The fresh-seed rebuild-time saving must exceed 50%, and partitions reused across a link retry must still be valid after concurrent weak-winner changes. Validating a partition’s dependency fingerprint against the committed resolution snapshot is intended to allow reuse where it remains sound, but the proposal alone establishes neither the saving nor the absence of stale reuse.
Does “above 50%” include exactly 50%?
No. “Above 50%” is strict: exactly 50% would not meet that wording. The saving is a reduction in rebuild time relative to full LTO, not a program-runtime percentage.
What does “recover” mean in this question without claiming that the recovery has happened?

It describes the outcome being sought in the fresh-seed rebuild comparison. Reusing partitions that still validate across retries might avoid rebuilding work, but whether the resulting saving exceeds 50% is unknown until measured. The question does not report a new timing result.
Could I assume that every link retry currently recompiles every partition?

No. The question concerns the potential benefit of retaining validated partitions across a retry; it does not state how much work any particular retry currently repeats. An assumption that all partitions are recompiled would add an unsupported fact.
If a partition was unchanged before a weak-winner change, why might its reuse still be unsafe?

Its cached optimized code may rely on a resolution condition that the weak-winner change affects. Being unchanged as a stored partition does not establish that its binding assumptions remain applicable. Validation against the committed snapshot is meant to distinguish a genuinely reusable partition from one whose recorded dependencies no longer hold.
So does snapshot validation mean that the partition merely has to exist in the cache?

No. Cache presence and validity are different. The proposed reuse requires checking the partition’s dependency fingerprint against the committed snapshot for the link that will use it. A stored partition that fails that check must not be admitted to the final linked result on the strength of its earlier cached state.
What does ‘committed’ contribute when weak-winner changes happen concurrently?

It identifies the consistent resolution view against which reuse is judged for the final link. Comparing a partition with an earlier view would not settle whether its assumptions still apply after relevant concurrent changes. The question does not prescribe how the snapshot is committed or how concurrent publications are ordered.
Would using any recent snapshot be close enough?

Not necessarily. The relevant comparison is with the committed snapshot that governs the final link, not just a snapshot that seems recent. If the selected snapshot and the final link’s resolution conditions differ in a way that matters to a cached partition, calling the partition valid from the earlier comparison could admit stale work.
Is an epoch change itself proof that every cached partition has gone stale?

No. An epoch change signals that the link’s resolution view needs reconsideration. It does not show that every partition depends on the changed weak-winner binding. The proposed validation offers a way to retain partitions whose fingerprints still hold while rejecting ones whose assumptions do not.
Conversely, does retrying the link automatically cure a stale partition?

No. A retry gives the build an opportunity to work from an applicable resolution view; it cannot make an invalid cached assumption correct merely by repeating the link. The dependency fingerprint must validate against the committed snapshot before the partition is reused in the final link.
Does a matching fingerprint always establish sound reuse?

Only if that fingerprint captures the dependencies the cached partition actually relies on, and the comparison uses the relevant committed conditions. A match cannot detect a weak-winner dependency that was omitted from the fingerprint. The question asks whether the proposed validation can avoid stale reuse; it does not assert that fingerprint coverage is already complete.
What does ‘admitting stale partitions’ specifically mean?

It means permitting cached optimized partitions into the final linked result even though a concurrent weak-winner change has made an assumption embodied in them invalid. A partition might still be stored in the cache; the concern is accepting it for this link without sound validation.
Would a partition that remains stored but is rejected at final link count as admitted?

No. Retaining a cache entry for possible consideration is different from using it in the final result. If validation rejects it before final linking, it has not been admitted to that link on the basis of stale assumptions. The question does not define a cache-eviction policy.
What if the weak-winner change is unrelated to the partition’s symbol dependencies?

Then that change alone need not disqualify the partition, provided its relevant fingerprint still validates against the committed snapshot and its other reuse conditions hold. Selective reuse is the potential source of rebuild savings; treating every weak-winner change as affecting every partition would discard that opportunity.
Could an apparently unrelated change become relevant through a dependency chain?

Yes, conceptually. A cached partition may depend indirectly on resolution information associated with the changed binding. The validation has to cover the relevant dependency relationship; calling a partition unrelated solely because it does not directly name the weak symbol would not establish safety.
Does the question require every unchanged partition to be reused across every retry?

No. It asks whether snapshot-validated retry reuse can raise fresh-seed savings above 50% without stale partitions. A partition whose dependencies fail validation must not be used simply to improve the savings figure. The question leaves the number of reusable partitions and the number of retries unstated.
Could a correct implementation still fall short of the rebuild-savings threshold?

Yes. Rejecting unsafe reuse can preserve soundness while leaving too much rebuild work to achieve a saving above 50%. The timing condition and the no-stale-partitions condition must be assessed separately; satisfying one does not imply the other.
Could a result above 50% answer the entire question if we do not know whether cached partitions were valid?

No. The question requires both performance and sound reuse after concurrent weak-winner changes. A measured saving above 50% would not justify accepting a partition whose dependency fingerprint no longer validates against the committed snapshot.
What would clean-build trace agreement tell us in this context?

Agreement with corresponding clean-build traces would provide behavioral evidence for the concurrent-change cases compared. It would not alone list every partition reused or prove the fingerprint covers every possible weak-winner dependency. Equally, a favorable rebuild-time measurement cannot stand in for a semantic comparison.
If the observed traces match, can we say no stale partition was admitted anywhere?

Not universally. Matching traces show agreement for the observed behavior in those comparisons. They may support the soundness assessment for those cases, but do not independently prove that every possible stale partition was excluded or that all dependencies were represented.
Does the question ask us to change the rule on inlining preemptible definitions to get above 50%?

No. Snapshot-validated retry reuse is about retaining cached partitions whose assumptions still hold. It is not permission to inline a preemptible definition or to ignore symbol-resolution changes in the interest of rebuild speed.
Would reusing a partition with a validated resolution fingerprint settle its inline-body dependencies too?

Not automatically. A resolution view and the dependencies of bodies incorporated into cached code are different validity concerns. Reuse is sound only if the partition’s relevant dependency fingerprint and any other applicable conditions actually cover what the cached optimization relies on. The question does not say those other dependencies may be ignored.
What if the snapshot validates before a further concurrent weak-winner publication?

The final link must not rely on a validation that ceased to apply before the resolution view it uses was committed. The question’s emphasis on checking against the committed snapshot is intended to avoid accepting a partition solely because it matched an earlier view. It does not specify a detailed ordering or retry procedure for multiple concurrent publications.
Do we know how often that sort of concurrent change will force a retry?

No. The question provides no counts of weak-winner publications, epoch changes, link retries, or reusable partitions. Those quantities cannot be inferred from the existence of the reuse proposal or the above-50% target.
Is there a numerical target for runtime in this particular question?

This question specifies a rebuild-time saving above 50% and asks that stale partitions not be admitted after concurrent weak-winner changes. It does not state a program-runtime measurement or a runtime threshold for this particular inquiry. Rebuild savings should not be confused with execution speed.
What would a positive answer require, stated without inventing a result?

It would require a fresh-seed rebuild-time comparison showing savings strictly greater than 50% relative to full LTO, together with evidence that partitions reused after concurrent weak-winner changes validated against the committed snapshot and did not carry stale assumptions into the final link. Neither finding is supplied by the question.
Can you answer the question as it stands, without predicting the measurements?

It is not established yet. Snapshot-validated retry reuse could retain unaffected partitions and improve fresh-seed rebuild savings, but whether savings rise above 50% while excluding stale partitions after concurrent weak-winner changes remains to be determined.
My hypothesis is that reusing partitions only when both their Merkle and resolution fingerprints match the committed epoch yields at least 50% rebuild savings and zero clean-build trace mismatches.

That is a prediction about conditional reuse, not a measured result. A cached partition would be accepted only if both its Merkle dependency fingerprint and its resolution fingerprint match the conditions associated with the committed epoch. The predicted outcomes are rebuild-time savings of at least 50% and zero mismatches against corresponding clean-build traces.
Why require both fingerprints to match? Wouldn’t the resolution fingerprint be enough after a weak-winner change?

The two fingerprints concern different assumptions. The resolution fingerprint addresses symbol-binding conditions, including those relevant to a weak-winner change. The Merkle fingerprint addresses dependencies of incorporated inline bodies. A partition could pass one check while depending on information covered by the other that has changed, so the hypothesis makes both matches prerequisites for reuse.
Does ‘both’ mean a partition may be reused if either fingerprint matches?

No. It means the Merkle fingerprint and the resolution fingerprint must each match. If either fails, the proposed rule does not justify reusing that cached partition for the link governed by the committed epoch.
What is the committed epoch doing in this hypothesis?

It anchors the validation to the resolution state committed for the link, rather than to an earlier view associated with a link attempt that was retried. The hypothesis does not specify how epochs are represented, how fingerprints are compared, or the mechanics of committing that state.
Is it enough for the fingerprints to match an epoch from before the retry?

Not under the stated rule. They must match the committed epoch applicable to the final link. A match against an earlier epoch would not establish that the partition’s assumptions remain valid after a relevant concurrent resolution change.
Does the epoch number itself contain the Merkle dependency information?

The hypothesis does not say that. It requires the Merkle and resolution fingerprints to match the committed epoch’s applicable conditions. Merely comparing an epoch number would not necessarily verify the dependencies of a cached inline body or the resolution assumptions the partition used.
Suppose the resolution fingerprint matches, but the Merkle fingerprint does not. What does the hypothesis say to do?

It says not to reuse that partition under this rule. Matching symbol-resolution information would not make a stale inline-body dependency current. The hypothesis does not prescribe the subsequent rebuilding procedure or say how many other partitions would be affected.
And if the Merkle fingerprint matches but the resolution fingerprint fails?

Again, the partition would not qualify for reuse. An unchanged incorporated body cannot justify carrying forward a binding assumption that does not match the committed conditions. The two checks are complementary rather than interchangeable.
Would matching both fingerprints prove that every possible cached dependency was captured?

No. A match supports reuse only if the fingerprints actually represent the assumptions on which the partition depends and are evaluated against the applicable committed state. A dependency omitted from both would not become detectable merely because the recorded values match. Completeness remains part of what the hypothesis needs to withstand evaluation.
Does the rule mean every partition must be rebuilt whenever an epoch changes?

No. An epoch change prompts validation against the committed conditions; it does not, by itself, mean every partition’s fingerprints fail. The hypothesis seeks to reuse partitions whose two fingerprints still match while withholding reuse from those that do not.
Could a partition whose source never changed still fail one of these checks?

Yes. A cached partition can embody dependencies on other bodies or on symbol resolution. Its own unchanged source is not proof that those external assumptions remain applicable. That is why the hypothesis conditions reuse on the fingerprints rather than source identity alone.
Does this permit inlining a preemptible definition if its resolution fingerprint matches?

No. A fingerprint match is a condition for reusing cached work; it does not make an unjustified inlining transformation sound. The rule against preemptible inlining remains a separate constraint, and this hypothesis does not relax it.
How should I interpret the at-least-50% rebuild-savings threshold?

It is an inclusive threshold: a measured saving of exactly 50% would satisfy this hypothesis’s rebuild-time condition, while anything below 50% would not. It concerns rebuild time relative to the full-LTO baseline, not execution time of the resulting program. No measured saving is provided by the hypothesis.
Does the hypothesis say the saving is a median across fresh-seed edits?

No aggregation method is stated in this hypothesis. It predicts at least 50% rebuild savings but does not specify a median, a per-edit guarantee, a sample count, or a particular benchmark run. Those details should not be inserted into the prediction.
Could I claim that every partition reuse will save 50% rebuild time?

No. The percentage is a predicted rebuild-time outcome for the approach, not a saving assigned to each partition or each reuse decision. The amount of work available to reuse and the effect on elapsed rebuild time are not quantified here.
What exactly does zero trace mismatches require?

For the comparisons used to evaluate the hypothesis, cached-path traces must agree with their corresponding clean-build traces, with no mismatches reported. The hypothesis supplies no number of comparisons or observed trace results, and trace agreement would concern the behavior observed in those comparisons, not byte-for-byte identical binaries.
Would matching traces tell us which partitions were reused or rejected?

No. Traces report observed program behavior. They do not, by themselves, list fingerprint matches, failed validations, cache hits, or rebuilt partitions. A zero-mismatch result and evidence that the proposed reuse rule was followed would be distinct observations.
If rebuild savings reach 50% but one clean-build trace mismatches, does the combined hypothesis hold?

No. It predicts both at least 50% rebuild savings and zero trace mismatches. Meeting the timing threshold cannot compensate for a semantic mismatch, and matching every observed trace cannot substitute for the required timing result.
Is the reverse also true if all traces match but rebuild savings fall below 50%?
Yes. The trace condition would be satisfied for the comparisons made, but the rebuild-savings condition would not. The hypothesis requires both outcomes together; neither is established yet.
Does this hypothesis include a resulting-program runtime slowdown target?

No. Its explicit outcomes are at least 50% rebuild savings and zero trace mismatches. Those measures do not supply a resulting-program runtime comparison. No runtime percentage should be attributed to this hypothesis.
Can we call it a demonstrated fix for concurrent weak-winner changes now?

No. It proposes a reuse gate intended to exclude stale partitions by requiring both fingerprints to match the committed epoch. Whether that produces zero clean-build trace mismatches under relevant changes, while saving at least 50% of rebuild time, remains to be tested.
State the hypothesis in one sentence without turning either target into an observed finding.
